narrative: Canada courts tech talent and offers a clear PGWP-to-PR route, but a four-year degree and softening salaries hold the return in the middle. International students can work up to 24 hours a week off campus during term and full time in scheduled breaks, then move onto a post-graduation work permit valid for up to three years. Twelve months of skilled Canadian work qualifies you for Express Entry through the Canadian Experience Class, and permanent residence often follows within a year or two, one of the clearest study-to-PR routes anywhere. Citizenship needs 1,095 days of physical presence, with pre-PR study time partly credited. Costs are moderate for the group, and the clear study-to-residence path is a big part of the appeal, even after recent study-permit caps and a higher proof-of-funds requirement.

narrative: Germany combines severe IT skills shortages, tuition-free study and strong pay for the best return in the set, if you can work in German. Students may work 140 full or 280 half days a year, then receive an 18-month residence permit to find graduate-level work. With an EU Blue Card and B1-level German you can reach a permanent settlement permit in as little as 21 to 33 months, and the 2024 reform cut the citizenship wait to five years (three with strong integration) while finally allowing dual nationality. The catch is language: many roles and daily life still run in German. Tuition-free public universities make Germany comfortably the cheapest of the eight, so even a modest starting salary produces an outstanding return on cost.

narrative: Singapore is a well-paid Asian tech hub with low tuition after the grant, but a three-year bond, no post-study visa and selective PR temper the visa score.
